metadata.title: Competitiveness, country economic inequality and adolescent well-being: Analysis of 60 countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students and applies sampling weights with sampling probabilities at both school- and student-level, following PISA technical notes. The analytic sample is restricted to adolescents with complete data on competitiveness and well-being and with available country Gini index values; participants from countries without Gini data are excluded. Missing covariates (age/sex, household socioeconomic status, immigration status) are handled via multiple imputation with chained equations (mice), and multilevel models are then estimated across imputed datasets with Rubin’s rules. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight usage cannot be confirmed from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable here because the dependent variables are non-cognitive well-being constructs (life satisfaction and purpose of life) derived from questionnaire items and standardized composite scores, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scales. The paper does report a missing-data strategy for covariates (multiple imputation with chained equations), so missingness is addressed, but PV handling is not part of the analysis pipeline for these outcomes.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used OECD PISA 2018 data for 15-year-old students. Included only adolescents with complete data on competitiveness and well-being and with available country-level Gini index values; excluded participants from countries without Gini index data. Further restricted to the final analytic sample of 347,934 adolescents from 60 countries (age mean 15.8; 50.7% girls). Missing covariates (age/sex, household socioeconomic status, immigration status) were imputed via multiple imputation with chained equations (mice) rather than listwise deletion.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel linear mixed modeling (random intercepts at individual and country levels). Individual competitiveness: β = 0.087 (95% CI 0.084 to 0.091), p < 0.001. Country competitiveness: β = 0.002 (95% CI −0.057 to 0.062), p = 0.938. Interaction: middle Gini significant (β = 0.022, 95% CI 0.004 to 0.039); high Gini not significant (Supplementary Table 3). Stratified strongest individual competitiveness association in middle Gini countries: β = 0.098 (95% CI 0.093 to 0.102).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged individual competitiveness, country competitiveness, and country inequality (Gini index) alongside age and sex to model life satisfaction, finding that higher individual competitiveness is positively associated with life satisfaction while country-level competitiveness is not. This indicates that interventions that strengthen students’ competitive engagement or motivation may support adolescent life satisfaction, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel linear mixed modeling (random intercepts at individual and country levels). Individual competitiveness: β = 0.214 (95% CI 0.211 to 0.217), p < 0.001. Country competitiveness: β = 0.115 (95% CI 0.058 to 0.172), p < 0.001. Interaction: middle Gini significant (β = 0.037, 95% CI 0.021 to 0.053); high Gini not significant (Supplementary Table 3). Stratified strongest individual competitiveness association in middle Gini countries: β = 0.227 (95% CI 0.222 to 0.231).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged individual competitiveness, country competitiveness, and country inequality (Gini index) alongside age and sex to model purpose of life, finding that both individual and country competitiveness are positively associated with purpose of life and that the individual-level association is strongest in middle Gini countries. This indicates that education and well-being policies may benefit from fostering constructive competitive climates and personal drive, while recognizing that the observed heterogeneity by national inequality is correlational rather than causal.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-sectional observational study uses OECD PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-olds, analyzing 347,934 adolescents from 60 countries with complete competitiveness and well-being data and available country Gini index values. Outcomes are non-cognitive well-being composites: life satisfaction and purpose of life, standardized across OECD countries. The authors estimate multilevel linear mixed models with random intercepts for individuals and countries, applying school- and student-level sampling weights and handling missing covariates via multiple imputation (mice) with Rubin’s rules. Results show that individual competitiveness is positively associated with both life satisfaction (β = 0.087) and purpose of life (β = 0.214), while country competitiveness predicts purpose of life (β = 0.115) but not life satisfaction. The association between individual competitiveness and well-being is heterogeneous by national inequality, with the strongest effects in middle Gini countries. Limitations include self-reported measures and cross-sectional design, so causality cannot be inferred.
